Adult Hip Dysplasia

Recon · 1 / 65

1Basics

Epidemiology

Definitionabnormal hip development → shallow acetabulum, deficient anterior + lateral coverage

IncidenceUS 3–5% · ~10% of all THA done for dysplasia · 48% of THA in patients <50 yr are for dysplasia

Most common cause of THA <50 yr (excluding osteonecrosis) — DDH
✗ Wrong options: FAI · SCFE · Perthes/MED · femoral neck fracture

Demographicsfemales > males (2–4× relative risk)

Risk factorsbreech, female, primiparity, family history

Pathophysiology

Mechanismundercoverage → load concentrated on superolateral acetabular rim → ↑ contact stress → degenerative labral tear, cartilage delamination → secondary OA

Labrumhypertrophied, intrasubstance tearing (labrum stabilises the hip → overloaded)

Arthritis timinguntreated → THA typically in 30s–40s

Anatomic abnormalities

Dysplastic hip
Acetabulum Shallow, lateralized, anteverted · deficient anteriorly + superiorly (superolateral) · may be retroverted with superolateral bone loss (OB)
Femoral head Small, aspherical
Femoral neck Short, ↑ anteversion (+5° to +16°, rises with subluxation) · coxa valga (↑ neck-shaft angle)
Greater trochanter Posteriorly placed
Femoral canal Small, narrow, straight · thick cortices
Contact area ↓ head–acetabulum contact area

"Most common abnormalities"✓ excessive femoral anteversion + posterior greater trochanter
✗ Wrong options: medialized acetabulum · large contact area · large head/long neck · ↓ neck-shaft angle

Femoral concern before THA → ✓ excessive anteversion
✗ Wrong options: osteopenia · varus · bowing · stove-pipe femur

Rotational deformity sitediaphysis between lesser trochanter and isthmus
✗ Wrong options: metaphyseal torsion

Normal valuesacetabulum anteversion 15°, abduction 45° · femoral neck anteversion 15° · neck-shaft angle 125° · head centre at level of greater trochanter

3Presentation

Symptomsinsidious groin/hip pain · worse with hip flexion or ER in weight-bearing · lateral hip pain + limp / Trendelenburg (abductor fatigue)

Exam↑ internal rotation in flexion (↑ femoral anteversion) · generalized laxity (Beighton) · ± FADIR pain (labral)

Anterior apprehension signlateral decubitus, hip extended, progressive ER + adduction → apprehension/pain

Prone external rotation testanterior force on posterior greater trochanter

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

ViewsAP pelvis, lateral, false-profile view

Findingsfemoral head asphericity · coxa valga · narrow femoral canal

CTpreoperative planning only (ordered by treating surgeon) · include distal femur if clinical anteversion · canal diameter over-estimated on AP, under-estimated on lateral

Diagnostic criteria – radiographic parameters

Measure View Dysplastic Borderline Normal
LCEA (Wiberg) — vertical through head centre vs line to lateral acetabular edge AP <20° 20–25° 25–39°
Tönnis angle (acetabular roof / sourcil inclination) AP >10° — <10°
ACEA (Lequesne) — anterior coverage False-profile <20° — 25–40° · >40° = FAI
FEAR index AP — — <5° = stable hip, no treatment
Extrusion index (uncovered head / head width) AP >27% suggests dysplasia (TO) — —

LCEA cut-off variantsOrthobullets <20° dysplastic, OB <25° dysplastic (LCEA or ACEA) · borderline/mild dysplasia 18–25° (OB) · Wiberg (TO): >25° normal, 20–25° uncertain, <20° pathological · CE angle reliable only >5 yr (TO)
✗ Wrong options: <12 yr

Tönnis angle = acetabular index / acetabular roof angleused in hip dysplasia (TO) · line teardrop-to-teardrop + line from medial to lateral edge of sourcil (weight-bearing subchondral condensation)
✗ Wrong options: genu varum · Blount · recurvatum

Paediatric acetabular indexHilgenreiner's line + acetabular surface · <25° after 6 months (TO)

Other TO anglesMCE (head centre → medial sourcil) · acetabular arc = LCE + MCE

Acetabular version signs (TO)

Normalslight anteversion · anterior wall projects medial to posterior wall · posterior wall descends through femoral head centre

Retroversionanterior wall lateral to posterior wall · signs: crossover sign, posterior wall sign, ischial spine sign (spine protrudes into true pelvis) · also narrow ischium, laterally protruding iliac wing

Crossover signanterior rim crosses posterior wall below superolateral margin → anterior overcoverage OR whole-acetabulum retroversion OR posterior deficiency — any alone or combined (TO)

Posterior wall signposterior wall runs medial to head centre → posterior deficiency

Posterior wall lateral to head centreprominent posterior wall → excessive anteversion

Coxa profunda vs protrusio (TO)

Coxa profunda Protrusio acetabuli
Relation to ilioischial line Acetabular fossa medial to line, head is not Femoral head crosses medial to line
Meaning Overcoverage or normal variant (women) Excess depth, overcoverage, pincer

Crowe classification

Grade Proximal displacement (% pelvic height) Femoral head subluxation
I <10% <50% of head vertical diameter (head–neck junction from inter-teardrop line)
II 10–15% 50–75%
III 15–20% 75–100%
IV >20% >100% (high dislocation)

Hartofilakidis classification

Type Head position Acetabulum
A — Dysplasia Within acetabulum despite subluxation Segmental superior wall deficiency · inadequate depth
B — Low dislocation False acetabulum superior to true Superior wall absent · inadequate depth
C — High dislocation Completely uncovered, migrated superior + posterior Complete deficiency · excessive anteversion of true acetabulum

5Management

Symptomatic adult hip dysplasia
  • Concentric, congruent, joint space preserved→PAO (Bernese/Ganz)
    • Retroverted acetabulum→reverse (anteverting) PAO
  • Unreduced / incongruous joint→salvage (Chiari, shelf)
  • Borderline/mild only→± arthroscopy + labral repair + capsular plication
  • End-stage OA→THA (cup in true acetabulum)
    • Lengthening >4 cm (Crowe IV)→+ subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy

Nonoperative

Supportiveweight loss, NSAIDs, activity modification, intra-articular injection · limited role (premature OA) · PT + steroid injection not for lasting relief in 20s

No remodellingtriradiate closes ~10 yr · at 18 yr no pelvic growth left
✗ Wrong options: "continued remodelling (observe")

Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) indications

Indicationsymptomatic dysplasia, adolescent/adult, concentrically reduced hip + congruous joint space · preserved ROM · minimum 2 mm joint space (OB) · best: very low VCE 0–15°, concentric through ROM

Typical stemyoung woman, LCEA ~15°, ACEA ~14–18°, Tönnis 15°, labral tear, no chondral lesion → ✓ Bernese PAO
✗ Wrong options: surgical dislocation + osteoplasty (for FAI) · proximal femoral osteotomy (paediatric/abnormal NSA) · Salter · THA (needs advanced OA)

Intraop testneed ≥90° flexion + 15° IR after correction, otherwise add femoral osteotomy (prevent FAI)

Advantageshyaline cartilage coverage · posterior column intact → WBAT · large multidirectional corrections · preserves external rotators · delays THA

Outcome92% survivorship at 15 yr avoiding THA · >90% at 10–15 yr · better long-term survivorship than arthroscopy (✓) · retroversion series: 10-yr survivorship PAO 79% vs rim trimming 23%

Secondary instabilityafter arthroscopic labral debridement, not after PAO

Techniquemodified Smith-Petersen approach · osteotomies of pubis (superior pubic root), ilium, ischium · avoids posterior column (fracture → pelvic discontinuity → plate)

Later THA after PAO↑ risk of retroverted cup

Reverse (anteverting) PAOacetabular retroversion: ✓ LCEA <20° + positive posterior wall sign
✗ Wrong options: LCEA 21° + negative PWS · LCEA 23° + Tönnis 8 · LCEA 30°

Pelvic osteotomy descriptions

Osteotomy Description Patient
Bernese / Ganz PAO Multiple cuts: pubis, ilium, ischium near acetabulum ✓ Skeletally mature
Salter Above acetabulum through ilium to sciatic notch · opening wedge · hinges on mobile symphysis / triradiate Immature
Pemberton From AIIS posteriorly → ends at ilioischial limb of triradiate Immature
Dega Acetabular roof → triradiate · incomplete pericapsular cuts · does not violate sciatic notch · volume-reducing Neuromuscular DDH
Chiari (salvage) Cut above acetabulum to sciatic notch, shift ilium laterally · relies on fibrocartilage metaplasia · shortens limb Incongruous joint
Staheli shelf (salvage) Extra-articular buttress of bone over subluxed head · fibrocartilage cover Incongruous joint

Salvage outcome84% survivorship at 17 yr (advanced OA endpoint) · poor with advanced DDH, head asphericity

Hip arthroscopy failure in dysplasia

Rolecontroversial · adjunct to PAO (chondral, labral, cam lesions; abandon PAO if major chondral damage) · contraindicated in moderate–severe dysplasia · alone only for borderline/mild (with labral repair + capsular plication)

Prevalencedysplasia in ~13% of hip arthroscopy patients (mostly borderline/mild)

Outcome vs no dysplasia✓ greater failure rate · accelerated arthritis (~⅓) · ↑ femoral head subluxation/migration · reoperation ~½ · inferior function · iatrogenic instability
✗ Wrong options: decelerated arthritis · ↓ subluxation · ↓ reoperation · greater improvement

Missed DDH in FAI patients → poor outcomes after arthroscopic osteoplasty

Hip resurfacing

IndicationCrowe I or II · cannot address LLD · 10% revision at 6 yr · higher revision/complications than general population · posterior approach · complication: femoral neck fracture

THA in dysplasia – cup coverage, shortening osteotomy, nerve palsy

Indicationend-stage OA secondary to dysplasia ✓
✗ Wrong options: hemiarthroplasty (acetabular arthritis) · redirectional osteotomies (best before arthritis)

Cup goaltrue acetabulum (low + medial) · small reamers 38–44 mm, small cup <50 mm · no jumbo cup (reams away columns, medial wall blow-out)

Coverage ruleuncemented cup OK if <30% uncovered → ✓ accept 25% superolateral uncoverage and proceed · insufficient coverage = <60–70% covered
✗ Wrong options: ↑ abduction to 60° (↓ coverage, ↑ wear) · breach medial wall · elevate hip centre · cement augments

Options for deficient coveragedownsize cup · medialize · elevate hip centre · trabecular metal / cement augments · superolateral bone graft · tantalum revision shells

Pseudoacetabulumin ilium, poor support · cup there → loosening, malposition, ilium fracture (avoid)

High hip centregains bony support but ↓ abductor tension, ↑ JRF, ↑ loosening, ↑ dislocation · bone poorer higher in ilium

Cemented cupPMMA poor in shear → high loosening (avoid)

Bearingavoid MoM in young · ceramic-on-PE longest survivorship, fewest complications (OB)

Femurmodular stems correct rotational deformity · trochanteric osteotomy aids exposure in Crowe III/IV

Femoral shortening & sciatic nerve palsy

Riskrestoring true hip centre in high dislocation → over-lengthening → sciatic palsy (peroneal division) → foot drop (TO)
✗ Wrong options: hip centre too inferior (concern is too superior) · over-medialization (over-lateralization is the concern) · acetabular fracture (less likely)

Thresholdlengthening >4 cm → palsy (Orthobullets, OB) · 2–4 cm associated with palsy (OB)

Muscle at risk✓ EHL (peroneal)
✗ Wrong options: quadriceps (femoral) · lateral gastrocnemius/tibialis posterior/FHL (tibial) · adductor magnus · semitendinosus

Prevention✓ subtrochanteric femoral shortening osteotomy · also corrects angular/rotational deformity · obviates GT osteotomy · proximal + diaphyseal-engaging fit, no extra hardware · alternatively downsize components
✗ Wrong options: upsizing

Not preventivehip extension + knee flexion during exposure (helps exposure only) · anterior approach (no ↓ palsy; ↑ femoral nerve risk) · ↑ offset (does not change length) · navigation · ↑ medialization · anterior retractor placement · EMG · hamstring/quadriceps lengthening · GT osteotomy with progressive shortening (↑ nonunion, needs hardware)

6Complications

Complication Fact
Sciatic palsy 10× ↑ incidence (5–15%) · lengthening >4 cm · peroneal division 80% · only 35–40% recover fully
GT osteotomy nonunion 29% · ↓ with subtrochanteric osteotomy + trochanteric advancement
Dislocation 5–10%, esp. high hip centre
Loosening ↑ with high hip centre cup · Crowe III/IV revision rates > non-dysplastic
Others Periprosthetic femur fracture · infection · neurovascular injury

Long-termhigher THA revision rate in dysplastic hips · Crowe I–II short-term = primary OA

Sciatic palsy risk factorsdysplasia, revision, female, post-traumatic OA, lengthening · causes: posterior-approach trauma, stretch, haematoma, cement heat

X vs Y

Adult hip dysplasia FAI
LCEA <20° Normal/↑ (pincer)
ACEA <20° >40° = overcoverage
Labrum Hypertrophied, rim overload Crushed/sheared
Surgery PAO Arthroscopy / surgical dislocation + osteoplasty
Arthroscopy alone Fails → instability Indicated
PAO Salvage (Chiari / shelf)
Joint Concentric, congruous Incongruous / unreduced
Coverage Hyaline cartilage Fibrocartilage (metaplasia)

How it's asked

"Young woman, LCEA 16°, Tönnis 15°, labral tear, cartilage intact — best surgery?"Bernese PAO
✗ Wrong options: surgical dislocation + osteoplasty · Salter · THA

"Which statement about osteotomies is true?"Bernese = multiple cuts in pubis, ilium, ischium
✗ Wrong options: Salter from AIIS (that is Pemberton)

"Dysplasia, 18 yr, labral tear — true statement?"PAO long-term survivorship > arthroscopy
✗ Wrong options: secondary instability after PAO · remodelling continues · Dega for retroversion

"Reverse PAO — imaging that led to decision?"LCEA 18° + positive posterior wall sign

"Hip arthroscopy with dysplasia vs without?"greater failure rate

"Most common femoral abnormality in DDH?"excessive anteversion + posterior greater trochanter

"Femoral concern on THA templating in DDH?"excessive anteversion

"Crowe IV THA — clinical scenario most likely?"over-lengthening the extremity (TO)

"Crowe IV THA — nerve supply of which muscle at risk?"EHL (TO)

"Foot drop after THA with large lengthening — what would have prevented it?"subtrochanteric femoral shortening osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: anterior approach · ↑ offset · upsizing stem

"Template shows 25% superolateral uncoverage — next step?"accept and proceed as templated (<30% OK)

"Crowe IV with pseudoacetabulum — preop planning?"subtrochanteric osteotomy to avoid foot drop
✗ Wrong options: cup in pseudoacetabulum · jumbo cup · MoM · cemented cup

"Most common cause of THA <50 excluding osteonecrosis?"DDH

"52-yr-old with dysplasia and secondary OA?"THA
✗ Wrong options: PAO · hemiarthroplasty

"Positive crossover sign indicates?"anterior overcoverage, retroversion or posterior deficiency — any alone or combined (TO)

"Medial acetabular fossa medial to ilioischial line, head not?"coxa profunda (TO)
✗ Wrong options: protrusio

"CE angle of Wiberg — true?"<20° abnormal (TO)
✗ Wrong options: only reliable <12 yr · Hilgenreiner–Perkin angle

"Tönnis angle used in?"hip dysplasia (TO)

Adult Limb Deformity & Correction

Recon · 2 / 65

1Basics

Epidemiology & aetiology

Causeschildhood growth impairment, metabolic bone disease, severe OA, trauma / malunion / nonunion

Demographicsno gender predilection · young → trauma / childhood growth abnormality · upper limb rare (elbow, wrist malreduction)

Pathoanatomyaltered anatomic axis → mechanical axis deviation (MAD) → abnormal contact pressure + ligament strain → degeneration → worsening alignment

Childhood causesBlount's, focal fibrocartilaginous dysplasia, proximal tibial physeal injury, Cozen's phenomenon, SED, femoral anteversion, LLD

Medical causesrenal osteodystrophy, rickets (vitamin D deficient, hypophosphataemic), OI, CP, neurofibromatosis

Site ruleadult genu varum → mostly tibial (CORA proximal tibia) · adult genu valgum → mostly femoral (CORA distal femur)

Anatomy

Proximal femurneck-shaft angle 130 ± 7° · anteversion 10 ± 7° · GT tip level with head centre (start of anatomic femoral axis)

Femoral anatomic vs mechanical axisdiffer by 5–7° · tibia: anatomic = mechanical if no deformity

Tibial tubercleanterolateral · triangular shaft

sMCLjust posterior to medial epicondyle → 6 cm below joint line · LCL — posterior to lateral epicondyle → fibular head

JLCA >2°soft-tissue (ligamentous) laxity

3Presentation

Pain by deformityvarus → medial knee pain · valgus → lateral knee pain

Examcoronal/sagittal deformity · femoral anteversion → IR >70° · residual ↑ external tibial torsion · LLD · hip/knee/ankle ROM, laxity

Intermalleolar distance >8 cmvalgus (OB)

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

Viewsweight-bearing full-length AP + lateral · patellae facing directly anterior (rotation) · tube 10 ft away at knee level · plus WB views of each segment

CTrotational malalignment · axial cuts for femoral version

Mechanical axis (limb)centre of femoral head → centre of ankle

Anatomic axesbisect medullary canal (femur from GT tip, exits just medial to distal femoral midpoint)

MADlateral to knee centre = valgus · medial = varus

LLDtop of femoral head → centre of ankle, compare sides · femur/tibia measured separately

Normal joint orientation angles

Angle Axis Normal
aMPFA Anatomic 84° (80–89)
aLDFA Anatomic 81° (79–83)
mLPFA Mechanical 90° (85–90)
mLDFA Mechanical 87° (85–90)
MPTA Both 87° (85–90)
LDTA Both 89° (86–92)
JLCA — 0–2° (femoral/tibial joint lines parallel)
PDFA (sagittal) — 79–83°
PPTA (sagittal) — 77–84°

Notationlowercase a = anatomic · m = mechanical

Deformity analysis – CORA

CORAintersection of proximal + distal mechanical axes when deformity is purely angular

Angulation + translationCORA moves from the axis intersection

Multi-level deformityunrecognized intermediate segment → CORA may lie outside bone

Osteotomy not at CORAinduces translation in addition to angulation

Proximity ruledeformity closer to joint → greater effect on that joint's angulation

Correction orderangulation → translation → length → rotation

Diagnostic criteria – varus vs valgus by angle

Varus (femoral source) Varus (tibial source) Valgus (femoral source)
Threshold mLDFA >90° or aLDFA >83° MPTA <85° mLDFA <85° or aLDFA <79° · MPTA >90° also valgus
MAD Medial Medial Lateral

OB trap valuesLDFA 88° = normal · LDFA 91° = slight varus · MAD 5–7° from femoral anatomic axis = normal

5Management

Adult limb deformity
  • Mild / minimal deficit / unfit→bracing (KAFO), poorly tolerated
  • Varus, CORA tibia (MPTA <85°)→valgus HTO (MOWHTO or LCWHTO)
  • Varus, CORA femur (mLDFA >90°)→valgus DFO (lateral closing wedge)
  • Valgus >12°, CORA femur→varus DFO (lateral opening / medial closing)
  • LLD >2 cm→gradual lengthening ~1 mm/day
  • Multicompartment OA→TKA ± extra-articular osteotomy

Nonoperative

Indicationssubtle deformity within normal parameters · minimal functional deficit · unfit for surgery

KAFOAFO + metal uprights + mechanical knee joint + two thigh bands · bracing poorly tolerated · little data on progression

Operative criteria

Procedure Indication
Derotational femoral osteotomy No absolute · excess femoral anteversion with <10° ER · patellar maltracking/instability · gait (difficulty running)
Valgus-producing HTO Varus MAD + MPTA <85°, CORA in tibia · no arthritis in other 2 compartments · young, not TKA candidate
Valgus-producing DFO Varus MAD + mLDFA >90° / aLDFA >83°, CORA in femur · joint-line obliquity after HTO in combined deformity
Varus-producing DFO Valgus MAD + mLDFA <85° / aLDFA <79° · valgus >12° · no medial compartment arthritis · age <50 · isolated lateral OA · relative: genu valgum with ↑ Q angle, MCL stress
Gradual lengthening LLD >2 cm (not absolute)
TKA Deformity with multicompartment arthritis

Derotational femoral osteotomy

Sitesproximal (intertrochanteric/subtrochanteric, blade/locking plate — also corrects flexion/extension + varus/valgus) · diaphyseal (IM nail) · distal supracondylar (medial subvastus, locking plate)

Diaphyseal IM techniquederotate to 45° ER + 45° IR with patella in line/slightly ER relative to ASIS

Outcomeall forms improve outcomes · ideal correction debated · may alter coronal alignment

Complicationsundercorrection · overcorrection → retroversion + out-toeing (rare)

Valgus-producing tibial osteotomy (HTO)

Medial opening wedge Lateral closing wedge
Approach Anteromedial Anterolateral
Steps Biplanar guide · hinge pin medial → lateral just below lateral plateau · protect patellar tendon · pack wedge Resect anterior fibular head · cut proximal to tuberosity · medial cortex = hinge · staples/plate
Slope ↑ tibial slope ↓ tibial slope
Correction May lose correction over time —

HTO outcome90–95% excellent at 5 yr → 50–70% at 10 yr · 15–25% need TKA within 10 yr · worse: smokers, age >60, other-compartment OA, obesity, prior failed arthroscopy, insufficient correction

Distal femoral osteotomy – indications & outcomes

Valgus-producing DFOlateral closing wedge · K-wires aimed at far medial cortex just above MFC · hinge through medial cortex without perforating → intact medial cortex = ↑ axial + rotational stability

Varus-producing DFO✓ lateral opening wedge (leave 1–2 cm medial hinge, spacer + lateral plate) or medial closing wedge (metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, medial locking plate)
✗ Wrong options: lateral closing / medial opening (those make valgus)

Candidate for lateral opening wedge DFO✓ young (35-yr) runner, isolated lateral joint-line pain, mechanical axis through fibular head
✗ Wrong options: PF/anterior pain · tricompartmental OA → TKA · prior MPFL/TTT anterior pain · varus/medial pain

37-yr-old, 15° valgus, early lateral OA, failed NSAIDs + unloader brace → ✓ lateral opening wedge DFO
✗ Wrong options: lateral closing DFO + MOWHTO (varus) · HTO (varus) · TKA (too young)

Survival✓ 15-yr survival ~50% (failure 48.5%) · high mid/long-term deterioration + conversion to TKA

Better outcomehigher preoperative function
✗ Wrong options: lower function

TKA after varus DFOconventional components if bone stock adequate
✗ Wrong options: stemmed/constrained in most

Gradual limb lengthening

Distraction osteogenesislatency 5–7 days, then ~1 mm/day

Devicesexternal fixator (uniplanar, circular/hexapod) · lengthening IM nail ± ex-fix (for angular correction)

OutcomeLLD to <1 cm · can correct small diaphyseal/metaphyseal angulation

Complicationsex-fix: pin-site infection, scarring, cosmesis · IM: poor regenerate, joint contracture/dislocation, nail failure

TKA with deformity

Goalneutral mechanical alignment via distal femoral + proximal tibial cuts · valgus cut angle 4–7° (IM guide on AAF) · tibial IM = EM guides (AAT = MAT)

Extra-articular deformitylocate CORA · CORA further from knee → easier intra-articular correction · severe or close-to-joint deformity → extra-articular osteotomy + TKA · osteotomy better tolerated on tibia (equal effect on flexion/extension gaps)

Constraint↑ constraint / stems if collaterals compromised (laxity, prior osteotomy)

Outcomeconsistent improvement · results less reliable after prior extra-articular osteotomy

6Complications

Complication Fact
Under/overcorrection Unfavourable compartment loading · opening wedge may lose correction
Nonunion ~5% · risk: smoking, age >60, obesity, far-cortex hinge fracture
Patella baja Proximal tibial osteotomy · supra-tubercle > infra-tubercle · pain, harder future TKA
Tendon injury Quadriceps → femoral osteotomy · patellar tendon → tibial osteotomy
Infection 1–4% · ↑ nonunion · risk: smoking, inpatient admission
DFO-specific Lateral opening: quadriceps tendon injury, intercondylar fracture (too distal), lateral hinge fracture (↓ stability) · closing: medial hinge fracture

X vs Y

Varus-producing DFO Valgus-producing DFO
Treats Genu valgum, lateral OA Genu varum with femoral CORA
Wedges Lateral opening or medial closing Lateral closing (medial hinge)
Criteria mLDFA <85°, valgus >12°, age <50 mLDFA >90°
Genu varum (adult) Genu valgum (adult)
Usual CORA Proximal tibia Distal femur
Pain Medial Lateral
Osteotomy HTO DFO

How it's asked

"Young man, 15° valgus, early lateral OA, failed brace — best surgery?"lateral opening wedge DFO
✗ Wrong options: HTO · TKA

"Varus-producing DFO — true?"15-yr survival ~50%
✗ Wrong options: lateral closing/medial opening · age >50 medial OA · needs constrained TKA later

"Lateral opening wedge DFO — which patient?"35-yr-old runner, isolated lateral pain, axis through fibular head

"16-yr-old, intermalleolar distance 10 cm, lateral opening DFO planned — alignment?"MAD lateral to knee centre
✗ Wrong options: LDFA 88° normal · LDFA 91° varus

"Normal anatomic–mechanical femoral axis difference?"5–7°

"Valgus HTO indication?"MPTA <85°, CORA in tibia, other compartments spared

"Order of correcting deformity?"angulation, translation, length, rotation

"Osteotomy away from CORA causes?"translation

"Opening wedge HTO changes tibial slope?"↑ slope (closing → ↓)

"Distraction osteogenesis protocol?"5–7 day latency, 1 mm/day

Arthroplasty Preoperative Medical Optimization

Recon · 3 / 65

1Basics

Overview

Five domainsmedical optimization · preoperative counselling · VTE prophylaxis · anaesthesia plan · pain management plan

Goalidentify modifiable risk factors for postoperative complications

Genes & lab markers

HbA1cscreen hyperglycaemic patients · HbA1c >6.7 → ↑ wound complications · target roughly <8 (varies by surgeon/hospital)

Nicotine testingpreoperative, to confirm cessation

Patellar Clunk Syndrome

Recon · 17 / 65

1Basics

Epidemiology

Prevalence3.5% (mean) · up to 18% (12–21%) of PS TKAs (TO) · rarer with newer designs

Timingaverage 12 months (Orthobullets) · 7–11 months (OB) · 3–12 months, occasionally up to 3 yr (TO) · more with patellar resurfacing

First describedHozack 1989 (TO)

Pathophysiology

Lesionfibrous nodule at superior pole of patella / posterior surface of distal quadriceps tendon (suprapatellar, articular side)
✗ Wrong options: inferior pole

Mechanismnodule entrapped in intercondylar box during flexion → jerked out during active extension → painful clunk at 30–45° (~40°)

Causetrauma to quadriceps tendon at patellar resection · impingement of tendon on sharp anterosuperior edge of the box · abrupt transition ridge between box and trochlea

Risk factors

Category Factors
Preoperative Patella baja / short patellar tendon · valgus alignment · fibrosynovial proliferation at quadriceps insertion (resect it) · previous knee surgery / revision
Patellar component Small button · placed low (distal) — exposes superior pole · over-resection / thin button (↓ quadriceps offset) · uncovered cut bone (resect lateral facet) · implant overhang at distal pole
Femoral component PS design · ↑ posterior condylar offset · smaller (undersized) femur · flexed femoral component (posterior IM entry point — anterior femoral bow) · high intercondylar box ratio (trochlea extends proximal + anterior) / larger box
Other Thick PE insert (raises joint line → relative baja) · excessive distal femoral resection · anterior tibial tray · forced flexion

Intercondylar box ratio (ICBR)box height ÷ AP height of femoral component · high ICBR → earlier quadriceps contact → ↑ clunk · low ICBR favourable

Preventionlow-ICBR design · side-specific femur (7° oblique groove) · trochlear deepening + lengthening · exact sizing · avoid downsized/flexed femur (anterior IM entry point) · avoid anterior tibial tray · patellar button as proximal as possible, not beyond superior border · avoid over-resection/thin button · neutral or posterior tibial tray

3Presentation

Symptomspatellofemoral pain · popping, catching · may be painless

Exampalpable "pop"/"catch" as knee extends from flexion at ~40° (30–45°)

I Isolated suprapatellar fibrous nodule (true PCS)

III Nodule + generalized hypertrophic synovitis

  • Severe or failed nonop→arthroscopic nodule resection
  • Failed arthroscopy / component problem→open excision ± patellar revision

✗ Wrong options: rest/NSAIDs · patellectomy · patellar revision · lateral release/realignment

Open excisionfailed arthroscopy · planned component revision / realignment · limited lateral incision under local

✗ Wrong options: lateralized tibial tray (moves tubercle medially, helps) · lateralized femur (moves trochlea laterally, helps) · femoral ER

5Management

Confirmed PJI
  • Acute postop (<3–4 wk) or acute haematogenous (symptoms <3–4 wk)→DAIR + modular exchange

  • Chronic (>4 wk), fit host→two-stage exchange (gold standard)
    • Low-virulence, healthy host, no sinus→one-stage (Europe)
  • Positive intraop cultures at aseptic revision (≥2/5)→6 wk IV antibiotics
  • Unfit / refuses→suppression · salvage: resection, fusion, AKA

Definitionmacrophage-induced inflammatory bone loss → implant loosening without infection

Paingroin (cup), thigh (stem), knee · activity related · start-up pain (first steps) = loose femoral stem

Mode Mechanism
I — Pistoning ✓ Stem subsides within cement (or stem + cement within bone) · linear lucency around stem and cement · commonest · poor cementing
II — Medial midstem pivot Proximal stem medial, distal stem lateral · weak calcar support
III — Calcar pivot (distal toggle) Distal tip toggles medial–lateral ("windshield wiper") · poor distal support
IV — Bending cantilever (fatigue) Proximal support lost, distal fixed → stem fracture

6Complications

Heterotopic ossification

Frequencycommon radiographic finding (first year), rarely functional · ~15% clinically significant stiffness (Brooker III/IV) · more after THA than TKA · 2–5% despite prophylaxis

Biologymesenchymal cells in muscle/fascia → osteoblasts · starts within 16 h of insult, matures over >1 yr into lamellar bone

Risk factorsprolonged surgery · excessive soft-tissue handling · hypertrophic OA · ✓ male · ✓ ankylosing spondylitis · prior HO (other site or contralateral hip) · DISH · traumatic brain injury

Brooker grade Clinical significance
I–II Usually asymptomatic, inconsequential (I not a pain source)
III–IV Clinically significant stiffness, may need excision

HO prophylaxis

Method Regimen
NSAIDs Indomethacin classic (other NSAIDs equivalent) · 7–21 days (≥10 days; longer no benefit) · not 2 days · not in renal insufficiency/warfarin
Radiation 600–800 cGy (700–800 as effective as higher) · Orthobullets: within 24–48 h post-op · OB: within 24 h pre-op or 72 h post-op · Iorio/Healy: ≤6 h pre-op or ≤4 days post-op · pre-op = post-op efficacy (73% vs 76%)
Not effective Drains · etidronate (EHDP) — delays mineralization only · radiation 1 week before surgery · 1,500 cGy (unnecessary)

Answersprior HO + renal insufficiency + warfarin → ✓ 800 cGy pre-op on morning of surgery (✗ Wrong options: indomethacin 3–6 wk · 400 cGy day 2 · no treatment) · ankylosing spondylitis → ✓ pre-op radiation 700 cGy (✗ Wrong options: sciatic monitoring · 1,500 cGy · CPM · soft collar) · contralateral HO → ✓ radiation 8 h post-op (✗ Wrong options: indomethacin 2 days · drains · EHDP · RT 1 week pre-op)

Prophylaxis candidates (Purcell–Lachiewicz)bilateral hypertrophic OA · OA + lumbar DISH · AS · HO after contralateral hip surgery

HO treatment

Early Brooker III at 6 weeks, asymptomatic → ✓ observe, repeat X-ray in 6 weeks
✗ Wrong options: indomethacin (too late) · RT (too late) · excision at 10 wk (immature, ↑ recurrence)

Formed HOprophylaxis ineffective · ✓ only surgical excision eradicates

Excisionsevere loss of motion · wait ≥6 months for maturation + capsule · confirm maturity: stable serial films, normal bone scan uptake, normalized serum ALP (non-specific) · pre-op CT for resection planning · perioperative RT or NSAIDs after excision ✓ (mature grade III/IV + severe limitation → excision + post-op irradiation) · instability after excision common → have constrained liners available · protect sciatic nerve

Stiffness at 6 months with HO → ✓ first check ALP, ESR, CRP (exclude PJI, assess maturity)
✗ Wrong options: late indomethacin/RT · immediate excision · excision + constrained revision

Squeaking

Definitionhigh-pitched audible sound with hip motion (e.g. extension from flexion on stairs)

IncidenceCoC 0.5–10% · MoM 4–5% · revision for squeaking 0.5%

Causesimpingement · edge loading · component malposition · loss of fluid-film lubrication · third-body particles · thin flexible titanium stem · ✓ NOT subclinical infection

Painless squeak, well-positioned implants → ✓ observe
✗ Wrong options: revise to PE · change cup abduction

✗ Wrong options: same osteolysis as MoP · noisy hips ↑ osteolysis · fractures eliminated

✗ Wrong options: torsion · pistoning · subsidence

Type Incidence

Intraoperative femur Postoperative femur

Type Description Treatment
AG Greater trochanter · often osteolysis <2 cm displaced → nonop, partial WB, limit abduction · >2 cm (TO: >2.5 cm) → ORIF claw plate / cables / TBW · address osteolysis
AL Lesser trochanter Nonoperative (ORIF if large medial cortex — TO)
B1 Around/just below stem, well-fixed ORIF — locking plate + cerclage cables ± strut
B2 Around/below stem, loose, good proximal bone ✓ Revision to long porous-coated cementless (or tapered fluted) stem bypassing 2 cortical diameters + fixation of fragments
B3 Loose + poor / comminuted proximal bone PFR (elderly, low demand) · APC / proximal femoral allograft (young) · tapered fluted stem + struts
C Well below stem ORIF plate, leave arthroplasty alone

TO"Vancouver type 2" → ✓ shaft around stem
✗ Wrong options: GT · LT · distal

Type Location · subtype Treatment
A1 Proximal metaphysis · cortical perforation Bone graft (reamings)
A2 Proximal · nondisplaced crack (calcar) ✓ Cerclage before inserting stem
A3 Proximal · displaced unstable Fully porous-coated or tapered fluted stem
B1 Diaphyseal perforation (cement removal) Fully porous stem bypassing 2 cortical diameters ± strut

B3 Diaphyseal displaced Fully porous stem bypassing ± strut

Problem Key facts
Hypertension >140/90 · check reversible causes (missed meds, pain, anxiety, constipation) · oral agents preferred
Hypotension SBP <90 or drop ≥40 · ✓ commonest cause: intravascular volume depletion · hold antihypertensives, IV fluids ± CBC/BMP, ECG, troponin, CXR, CTPA
Hypoxia ↓ cardiac output + O₂ uptake · incentive spirometry for all · consider ischaemia, COPD, CHF, PE · keep SpO₂ >90% · distress → ICU
↓ Urine output Hypovolaemia, urinary retention, AKI · retention → straight cath, ↓ anticholinergics/opioids, tamsulosin · AKI → fix cause, euvolaemia, stop nephrotoxins
Altered mental status Find cause · reorient, normalize sleep–wake cycle
Chest pain Troponin + ECG if cardiac · aspirin + cardiology (ischaemia) · NSAIDs (pleuritic/wall) · PPI (dyspepsia)
PONV Opioids, anaesthetics · antiemetics, fluids, electrolytes
Ileus NG tube may be needed
Fever POD 1–2 cytokine fever — observe if well · after POD 3 → infectious (UTI, cellulitis, pneumonia, C. diff) or non-infectious (PE, withdrawal, transfusion/drug reaction) · antibiotics only for an identified source

Criteriaindependent ambulation with aid 50–100 ft · independent transfers · independent ADLs · 2 stairs with supervision · follows dislocation precautions · adequate home help

THA Pseudotumor (Metal on Metal Reactions)

Recon · 30 / 65

1Basics

Definition & epidemiology

Pseudotumour = ALVAL (aseptic lymphocyte-dominant vasculitis-associated lesion) — mass-forming tissue reaction to MoM wear · (semi-)solid or cystic periprosthetic mass ≥2 cm not due to infection, tumour, bursa or scar (TO)

Incidence10–15% of MoM THAs · resurfacing 0–39% (OB) · ALVAL ~0.3% (TO) · 45–50% of MoM revisions are for pseudotumour/ALTR · **~40% asymptomatic** · revision for symptomatic pseudotumour only 1.7–5.6%
✗ Wrong options: majority

Seen with✓ MoM THA / resurfacing (TO) · also MoP with head–neck (trunnion) corrosion → ALTR

Risk factors

Risk factors Not risk factors
↑ Cobalt + chromium (Co >5 µg/L — TO) ✓ BMI >40 (TO EXCEPT)
Female Metal allergy (TO)
High cup inclination >55° / ↑ anteversion → edge loading Obesity
Age <40 (TO) —
Taper/trunnion corrosion even with good position —
Large metal heads (some studies), low diametral clearance —

Pathophysiology

Two mechanismshypersensitivity to metal ions · local high wear debris · ✓ pseudotumour associated with ↑ linear wear of both components

Hypersensitivity✓ type IV delayed (cell-mediated) · metal ions form haptens with native proteins · ✓ lymphocyte-mediated in metal-allergic patients (jewellery reactions) (✗ Wrong options: macrophage-mediated · large/small particle wear) · ALVAL due to ✓ hypersensitivity to metals (✗ Wrong options: abrasion of shell · screws · stem corrosion)

Cells — conflictOrthobullets/OB: macrophages + lymphocytes in all, lymphocytes predominant · high-wear cases → more macrophages, smaller lymphoid aggregates · TO: metal debris cytotoxic to macrophages → macrophage depletion → lymphocyte predominance · OB (DTH): effector = T-cell but most participating cells are macrophages (lymphocytes ~5%)
✗ Wrong options: macrophage predominant

Histologydense perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate (hallmark), T and B lymphocytes, lymphoid follicles/aggregates, histiocytes, giant cells, necrosis · ✓ dark areas = T + B lymphocyte infiltrates (✗ Wrong options: particle-laden macrophages (typical of MoP)) · MoP trunnion ALTR → ✓ predominance of perivascular lymphocytes (✗ Wrong options: neutrophils (PJI) · lipid-laden histiocytes/giant cells (PVNS))

ALVAL true (TO)B lymphocytes · macrophage depletion · lymphoid aggregates · ✓ false: "diagnosis is not made by macroscopic appearance" (solid mass visible) · definitive diagnosis histological

3Presentation

Historygradual or sudden groin pain · may be asymptomatic · mass causing discomfort

Examperiprosthetic soft-tissue mass · Trendelenburg gait (abductor destruction) · groin pain with flexion, IR, adduction or rising from chair · NV usually normal

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

RadiographsAP pelvis + AP/lateral hip · exclude fracture · calcar erosion

MARS MRI✓ test that best correlates with prognosis (TO) (✗ Wrong options: ESR/CRP/WBC · metal ions (don't correlate) · CT (bone loss only)) · ✓ best test for painful MoM (✗ Wrong options: CT · bone scan · ion levels alone) · findings: periarticular fluid collection / solid mass, synovial/capsular hypertrophy, tendon avulsion, bone oedema · T1 ≈ bladder (transudate) · T2 hyperintense (hypointense foci = necrosis/metal) · MAVRIC, SEMAC newer

CTbony destruction, need for structural graft/augments

Genes & lab markers

Metal ions (Co, Cr)peak 12–24 months (run-in) then fall · >7 ppb (µg/L) → MARS MRI · ions renally excreted · activity does not change levels · Co:Cr ≈ 1:1 = MoM bearing, high Co:Cr (2:1) = trunnionosis
✗ Wrong options: pseudotumour

Aspirationdistinguishes metallosis from PJI · "dishwater" fluid (grey, watery, hazy) · ✓ manual cell count (fibrinous debris falsely ↑ automated) · MoM PJI cut-off >4,350 WBC · ARMD → lymphocytes >40%; PJI → PMN >70% (e.g. WBC >3,000 with low PMN, high lymphocytes = ✓ pseudotumour hypersensitivity; ✗ Wrong options: bacterial PJI · large-particle PE disease)

PJI vs ALTRALTR raises ESR, CRP, synovial WBC and gives false-positive α-defensin → ✓ thorough work-up: cultures, manual WBC, %PMN (80% cut-off) · α-defensin remains valid in RA
✗ Wrong options: α-defensin alone diagnoses PJI · ESR/CRP confirm · ALTR excludes PJI

5Management

MoM THA follow-up
  • Asymptomatic, ions <7 ppb, normal films→observe (serial X-ray + ions)
  • Ions >7 ppb (even asymptomatic)→MARS MRI
  • Symptomatic + normal ions + normal MRI→close follow-up 3–6 months
  • Pain/↑ ions + pseudotumour (or progressive osteolysis)→revise to CoP
    • Abductor loss→constrained liner ± gluteus maximus transfer

Observation

Indicationwell-functioning, low ions, no pseudotumour · serial radiographs (wear, loosening)

Close follow-up allowed✓ symptomatic, Co 6 / Cr 5, normal ESR/CRP, MARS MRI normal
✗ Wrong options: asymptomatic with ions >7 (needs MRI) · symptomatic with fluid (revise) · asymptomatic + fluid + progressive osteolysis (revise)

Revision indications

Revise✓ MARS MRI with periarticular fluid + abductor destruction · painful MoM + ↑ ions + pseudotumour · delay → more soft-tissue damage
✗ Wrong options: CRP 6 · HO · aspirate 900 WBC · cobalt 5 ppb alone

Techniquerevise to ceramic-on-polyethylene · single- or two-stage (if infection concern) · lateral or anterior approach · bimodular (modular-neck) stem + monoblock cup → ✓ revise both components to CoP + I&D
✗ Wrong options: head/liner exchange (monoblock cup) · larger Co-Cr head · I&D alone · observe

Abductor deficiencyTrendelenburg gait → ✓ gluteus maximus transfer (extensor → abductor) ± constrained liner
✗ Wrong options: flexion contracture · medial migration (cup-cage) · psoas · ER weakness

Dislocation after head/liner exchange for pseudotumour → ✓ abductor insufficiency
✗ Wrong options: offset · larger head · vertical cup · impingement

Infected pseudotumourneutrophils on histology + ↑ ESR/CRP → debride, explant, spacer, systemic antibiotics

6Complications

Revision outcomebone loss, soft-tissue destruction, abductor deficiency → harder revision, worse function · ↑ dislocation + infection

After revisioninstability · deep infection · aseptic loosening · persistent psoas tendinitis · persistent metal reaction · 14–20% re-operated within 5 yr

Femoral nerve palsyrare (case reports) · decompress + revise to CoP

IIIB Rim loss 9 → 5 o'clock, "up and in" (superomedial), Köhler line broken, discontinuity Cup-cage, custom triflange, structural graft

Type II vs III (TO)hip centre migration <3 cm vs >3 cm · II has supportive columns (≥50% host contact), III lacks them

Type Defect

Paprosky femoral bone loss

Type Description Treatment
I Minimal metaphyseal loss Primary components
II Extensive metaphyseal, intact diaphysis Extensively porous-coated long stem

TO (FNB 2014)<4 cm diaphysis → ✓ IIIB: extensively porous-coated tapered stem + impaction grafting

5Management

Revision THA planning
  • Exclude infection (ESR/CRP → aspirate)→if PJI, staged
  • Well-fixed, well-positioned cup + wear/lysis→head + liner exchange ± graft
  • Acetabulum: ≥50% host support→porous cup/jumbo + screws ± augments
    • Discontinuity / <50%→cup-cage, triflange, column plating
  • Femur: Paprosky I → primary · II/IIIA → extensively coated · IIIB → tapered fluted · IV→PFR/APC

Acetabular reconstruction

Porous hemispherical / jumbo cup + screwsneeds ≥50% host bone · cup inferior + medial (↓ JRF) · cavitary defects → particulate graft · ✓ most reliable long-term for Paprosky II · jumbo may compromise posterior column, dislocation
✗ Wrong options: cemented all-PE (high failure) · cage · bilobed · bipolar in acetabulum (pain, erosion)

Paprosky IIC (medial wall), ≥50% stock, no discontinuity, normal centre → ✓ jumbo cup + screws + morsellized graft (most stable + cost-effective)
✗ Wrong options: cage · triflange · spacer · augments

Paprosky IIB → ✓ cementless hemispherical cup + screws

Paprosky IIIA (LLD 3.5 cm, Trendelenburg) → ✓ porous cup + metal augments + graft + screws (unitize augment–cup with cement)
✗ Wrong options: particulate graft alone (IIA/IIB) · triflange (IIIB) · cemented cup (shear failure) · 2-stage

AugmentsPaprosky IIB–C, IIIA–B · survivorship 94–100% (2 yr), 92–100% (5 yr), 92% (10 yr)

Reconstruction / antiprotrusio cage + structural graftrim <⅔, <50% stock · PE cemented into cage · allograft failure commonest complication · without cage 40–60% failure · major bone loss + medial wall penetration → ✓ reinforcement cage + graft
✗ Wrong options: jumbo

Non-contained bicolumn defects >50% of weight-bearing area → ✓ ilioischial reconstruction ring + structural corticocancellous graft (restores stock)
✗ Wrong options: morsellized graft + cup · bilobed · roof ring

Impaction grafting (acetabulum)contained cavitary defects + cemented PE · not for discontinuity

Cemented cupcement liner into a well-fixed shell · revision cemented cups fail (shear)

Pelvic discontinuity & triflange

Definitionseparation of superior ilium from inferior ischiopubic segment · AAOS IV / Paprosky IIIB · acute pain, cannot bear weight (e.g. RA) → ✓ pelvic discontinuity

Principlesreconnect ilium + ischium · bleeding bone contact with ingrowth surfaces · graft defects · stable construct until ingrowth

Option Indication
Column plating + hemispherical cup Acute discontinuity, minimal bone loss, healing potential
Cup-cage Chronic discontinuity, Gross IV/V segmental defects · ✓ displaced transverse periprosthetic acetabular fracture with medial migration · ✓ Paprosky IIIB + structural graft
Custom triflange (CTAC) Massive bone loss + chronic discontinuity · irradiated bone · iliac → pubic → ischial flanges, screws ± posterior column plate · ✓ most common complication: dislocation
Distraction Discontinuity with shell ± augments
Bulk allograft + cemented cup ~50% failure (resorption, infection)
Independent cage alone 50–60% failure

Triflange chosen because of✓ pelvic discontinuity (✗ Wrong options: dislocations · IPD · loosening · Paprosky 2B) · triflange needs posterior/extensile exposure (✗ Wrong options: anterior approach for ischial/iliac flanges) · not a bilobed cup

Paprosky IIIB with discontinuity → ✓ custom triflange or cup-cage (✗ Wrong options: cemented cup · multihole cup) · chronic discontinuity after infection cleared (6 months, normal labs) → ✓ triflange + femoral revision (✗ Wrong options: new spacer · bulk allograft · cage alone · Girdlestone)

Osteolysis & isolated liner exchange

Retain shell + liner exchange + graft lysis✓ well-designed, well-fixed modular cup with good locking mechanism and record · lysis via screw holes/dome hole; loosening late
✗ Wrong options: non-modular · instability · radiolucency · migration

Indicationseccentric PE wear with stable components · acute infection · trunnionosis

Typical answerseccentric head + proximal femoral lysis, fixed components → ✓ synovectomy + liner exchange (✗ Wrong options: stem/cup revision) · massive cup lysis, ceramic-on-conventional PE, fixed cup → ✓ liner exchange + grafting + switch head to METAL (✗ Wrong options: new ceramic head on used taper (fracture; metal sleeve if ceramic wanted)) · lysis around one screw → ✓ liner exchange + remove screw + debride ± graft (Beaulé: no lesion recurrence) · retroacetabular lysis with clicking, normal labs → ✓ head + liner exchange + retroacetabular graft

Osteolytic lesionsmay shrink/heal without grafting once wear source removed · grafting optional/controversial

Complication✓ dislocation (11–25%) · use larger head · damaged locking mechanism → cement liner into shell (2–4 mm mantle)

Ischial lysis with dissociated dome-hole eliminator → ✓ wear-induced osteolysis
✗ Wrong options: chondrosarcoma · metastasis · corrosion

Femoral revision

Primary componentsPaprosky I (no unexpected bone loss)

Extensively porous-coated long stem (or porous/grit combo) or modular tapered — Paprosky II, IIIA (IIIB modular fluted tapered) · 95% survival at 10 yr · bypass most distal defect by 2 cortical diameters · cavitary → particulate graft · cortical defects → struts/plates · ✓ superior to cemented revision

Typical answersloose hemi with proximal loss → ✓ cementless diaphyseal press-fit stem (✗ Wrong options: bone scan · tumour prosthesis · metaphyseal cement) · IIIA with fracture → ✓ fully coated cementless + cables + graft (✗ Wrong options: ORIF · modular · total femur) · start-up pain + subsidence, no defects → ✓ uncemented long fully porous stem (✗ Wrong options: cemented · APC · PFR · spacer) · deficient proximal femur with >4 cm isthmus → ✓ diaphyseal-engaging extensively coated (✗ Wrong options: standard cemented · proximally coated · PFR · APC) · <4 cm isthmus (IIIB) → ✓ modular fluted tapered stem (✗ Wrong options: struts alone · impaction + cementless (impaction needs cemented stem) · metaphyseal tapered) · early loosening at 3 months → ✓ non-modular tapered fluted Ti stem

Failed ingrowth signsreactive line around porous part · hypertrophy under collar · pedestal at tip (no stress shielding) → ✓ revise femoral component

Symptomatic loose osteolytic stem → ✓ protected WB + urgent (not emergent) revision when cleared
✗ Wrong options: reassure · alendronate

Impaction grafting (femur)ectatic canal, thin cortices · Paprosky IIIB, IV · morsellized fresh-frozen allograft + smooth tapered cemented stem · subsidence commonest complication

APCPaprosky IIIB, IV · allograft canal slightly larger than host · cement stem into allograft, press-fit 4–6 cm into host

EPR / PFRmassive loss, non-supportive diaphysis · elderly/sedentary · frozen section of osteotomy bone to exclude tumour · distal fixation cemented / compressive osseointegration / press-fit

Cemented revision stemsirradiated bone, severe osteopenia, Dorr C · high failure · remove old cement, neocortex, sclerotic bone

Indications✓ <4 cm diaphyseal cortex · extensive metadiaphyseal loss with <4 cm isthmus · Paprosky IV · failed multiple osteosyntheses of proximal femoral nonunion · elderly/sedentary · ✓ EXCEPT: age <50

Pre-op film indicating PFR✓ Paprosky IV (no isthmus) (II → extensively coated, IIIA → diaphyseal/modular tapered)

Extended trochanteric osteotomy

Useremove well-fixed stem / difficult cement mantle (✓ ETO when only half the cement can be removed) · 12–14 cm including vastus ridge · enables diaphyseal-engaging stem
✗ Wrong options: short metaphyseal stem · impaction on loose mantle · cement-in-cement on loose mantle · spacer

Proximal migration✓ plate + cables
✗ Wrong options: abduct >10–15° when fixing · <10 cm osteotomy (↑ migration) · distal prophylactic cable (prevents propagation only) · strut (junctional failure)

Gluteus maximus transfer (anterior part + TFL to GT) for irreparable abductors ✓ (label A) · Hardinge most associated with post-op Trendelenburg

Hemi in demented 91-yr-old dislocating → contributor ✓ dementia → convert to THA + constrained liner

MoM resurfacing with abducted cup, clunking → ✓ revise to conventional THA
✗ Wrong options: cup-only revision (leaves MoM)

Loose stem + well-fixed well-positioned cup, 10 dislocations, unknown implant, high-risk host → ✓ revise stem + cement constrained liner into existing shell (shell fixed, positioned, locking broken/unknown, room for 2–4 mm mantle)
✗ Wrong options: retrovert stem · remove all · Girdlestone

Conversion of hip arthrodesis

Indicationslow back + knee pain · ✓ gluteus medius function predicts ambulatory outcome (pre-op EMG)

THA Sciatic Nerve Palsy

Recon · 33 / 65

1Basics

Epidemiology

Incidence0–3% (OB ~1%; TO 0.6–3.7%, revision 7.6%) · by diagnosis (TO): primary OA 0.5%, DDH 2.3% (5.8% sciatic), revision 3.5% (3–8%)

Litigation✓ nerve injury = most common cause of THA malpractice litigation (38%) · LLD second (26%) · dislocation not reported · TO: suits arise mainly from failure to diagnose/manage the palsy

Nerves involved

Sciatic~80% (TO >90%) of THA nerve injuries · ✓ peroneal division almost always · peroneal: lateral, superficial, tightly packed fascicles, less connective tissue, tethered
✗ Wrong options: tibial (isolated only ~1%)

Anatomysciatic nerve closest to acetabulum at the ischium · care with posterior acetabular retractor when hip flexed

Approach (TO) Nerve at risk
Anterior LFCN (15–81%) > femoral > sciatic
Anterolateral / direct lateral Superior gluteal
Posterior Sciatic (peroneal)

Other nerves (TO)femoral (2nd commonest, 2.3% of injuries, ~0.8% of THAs) — anterior retractors, hyperextension, iliacus haematoma · obturator (rare) — cement extrusion through medial wall, anteroinferior screws → groin pain, medial thigh paraesthesia, adductor weakness · superior gluteal — medius split >5 cm above GT → Trendelenburg, often recovers

Causes

Mechanismsdirect trauma (retractor, laceration) · stretch (lengthening, lateralization, dislocation manoeuvres) · compression — haematoma, tight dressings · cement heat · unrecognized lumbar lateral recess stenosis ("double crush") · positioning (CPN in lateral position) · unknown ~40% (TO ≥50%)

Risk factors

✓ Risk factors Not risk factors
DDH ✓ (congenitally short neurovascular structures → over-lengthening) Obesity / BMI
Revision ✓ (highest) Rheumatoid arthritis
Female Osteonecrosis / AVN
Limb lengthening Male sex
Post-traumatic arthritis Anterolateral approach
Posterior approach Posterosuperior quadrant screws (safe zone)
Cementless femoral fixation DMARDs, chronic analgesics, low pre-albumin
Surgeon rating case as difficult ✓ (Eggli — only correlating factor) Coxa vara (no exploration needed)
Pre-existing lumbar stenosis / spine surgery —
Operative time ✓ · younger age · smoking · uncontrolled DM · VTE history · experienced surgeon, later case —

Lengthening thresholdsOrthobullets >4 cm · OB keep lengthening <3 cm · TO >3.8 cm peroneal at risk, >4 cm complete sciatic palsy

Sciatic explorationnot routine · advisable with distorted anatomy: ER deformity, protrusio, short head/neck, revision, DDH · ✓ not needed in coxa vara (TO)

3Presentation

Symptomsnumbness, paraesthesia in sciatic distribution · foot drop (no dorsiflexion, no EHL, weak eversion) · "slapping gait"

Prognosis by deficitworst: complete motor + sensory
✗ Wrong options: motor with intact sensation

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

CT / ultrasoundsuspected haematoma

EMGlater, to confirm level + guide prognosis · MRI of hip limited by artefact
✗ Wrong options: as immediate step

Foot drop with back pain, stable Hb, no swelling (POD 2) → ✓ lumbar lateral recess stenosis (double crush) → lumbar MRI
✗ Wrong options: positioning · haematoma · infection · VTE

Foot drop after therapeutic enoxaparin for PE + transfusions → ✓ haematoma compressing sciatic nerve
✗ Wrong options: mechanical · stenosis · embolic infarct · anaemia

5Management

New sciatic palsy after THA
  • Intraop (wake-up test / neuromonitoring)→extend hip, ↓ lengthening (subtrochanteric shortening)
  • Immediate post-op→hip extension + knee flexion; loosen dressings
    • Haematoma (drop in Hb, drainage, anticoagulated)→reverse + urgent evacuation
  • Persistent foot drop→AFO; tendon transfer (PTT) if AFO fails

Prevention – femoral shortening & nerve monitoring

DDHpre-op planning · lengthening <3 cm · ✓ subtrochanteric (femoral) shortening osteotomy · downsize components · intraop wake-up test · neurophysiologic monitoring
✗ Wrong options: anterior approach · modular components · larger head · acetabular osteotomy

Wake-up test shows no dorsiflexion with equal lengths in dysplastic hip → ✓ shortening subtrochanteric osteotomy
✗ Wrong options: EMG · continue + observe · spacer · neurology

Intraop MEP/EMG alert → ✓ extend the hip
✗ Wrong options: traction · flex hip (impinges on retractor) · extend knee · irrigation

Postoperative haematoma & other causes

Immediate palsy✓ hip extension + knee flexion (slackens nerve) · then search for reversible cause (axial imaging for haematoma)
✗ Wrong options: hip flexion + knee extension · flat bed NWB · EMG first · knee X-ray

Haematoma (warfarin INR 6, Hct drop, saturated dressing, complete palsy) → ✓ reverse INR + urgent surgical evacuation (I&D)
✗ Wrong options: VAC + monitor · transfuse + observe · switch to enoxaparin · IVC filter + exploration

Prognosis & management of foot drop

Recovery✓ only 35–40% regain full strength after complete palsy → 60–65% never fully recover (OB: 30–40%; TO: best series ~50%) · maximal recovery takes **~2 years**

Persistent foot drop✓ AFO first line (restricts plantarflexion in swing) · continue AFO at 4 weeks–3 months
✗ Wrong options: spine MRI · ankle fusion · revision THA · sural grafting · early tendon transfer · neurology first

AFO not tolerated, chronic → ✓ posterior tibial tendon transfer through interosseous membrane to lateral cuneiform (donor needs ≥4/5, loses 1 grade)
✗ Wrong options: ankle fusion · split TA transfer (TA 0/5) · peroneus longus (weak) · FHL + TAL

Retractor injury

DAA, foot drop + dorsal foot numbness after retractor slip → ✓ posterior acetabular retractor (4) · deep trochanteric retractor also risks sciatic · position 1 → superior gluteal · 2 → femoral (≈2 cm from anterior lip) · 3 → obturator

Obturator nerve injury (TO)

Persistent groin pain, no foot drop, no plantarflexion weakness, no Trendelenburg → ✓ obturator nerve
✗ Wrong options: femoral (anterolateral thigh) · sciatic (foot drop) · superior gluteal (Trendelenburg)

THA Stability Techniques

Recon · 34 / 65

1Basics

Four determinants of stability

1component design · 2 — component position · 3 — soft-tissue tensioning · 4 — soft-tissue function

Component design – head size & head-neck ratio

Head-neck ratiohead diameter ÷ neck diameter · ✓ larger ratio → greater arc of motion before impingement (primary arc) · ✓ larger head = most closely linked to ↑ ROM
✗ Wrong options: approach · extended offset · anteversion >18° · abduction <35°

Skirtsextend neck length but ✓ ↓ head-neck ratio → ↑ impingement + dislocation
✗ Wrong options: large ratio · 15° stem/cup anteversion · 50° abduction are safe

Jump distancetranslation before dislocation (~½ head diameter) · larger heads seat deeper → ↑ jump distance → ↑ stability

36 vs 28 mm head in revision✓ delays neck–socket impingement
✗ Wrong options: compensates abductor deficiency · ↓ volumetric wear (↑) · ↓ trunnion stress (↑) · compensates vertical cup

Large head will NOT compensate forabductor deficiency or vertical cup · ✓ high inclination negates the benefit of a larger head (dislocates with minimal translation)

Primary arc ↑ by✓ larger head
✗ Wrong options: collar · hooded liner · offset (affects JRF not arc) · more anteversion

Neck-shaft angle

Change vs native Leg length Offset
↑ NSA (valgus) ↑ ↓
↓ NSA (varus) ↓ ↑

Longer leg + less offset post-op → ✓ increased prosthetic neck-shaft angle
✗ Wrong options: medialized cup (↓ offset only) · standard offset stem (offset only) · longer neck (↑ both) · constrained liner

Trendelenburg + 3 dislocations + already long leg → ✓ more varus (high-offset) stem — ↑ offset without length
✗ Wrong options: skirt · longer neck · valgus stem · medialized cup

Acetabular liners

Elevated (lipped) rimplaced posteriorly ↑ stability · ↓ revision for instability

Lateralized (offset) liner+4–10 mm acetabular offset (+ small lengthening) · ↑ tension · ✓ ↑ acetabular component loosening (eccentric load, torsion at liner–shell + bone–implant interfaces, ↑ JRF + wear) — only liner type linked to early loosening

4Diagnosis & Classification

Component position

Component Target
Cup anteversion 5–25° (Lewinnek 15 ± 10)
Cup abduction (inclination) 30–50° (Lewinnek 40 ± 10)
Stem anteversion 10–15° (hard to adjust in cementless)
Combined anteversion 37° (stiff spine: 35–40°)

Approach adjustmentsposterior → more anteversion · anterior → less anteversion

Malposition Result
Excessive retroversion Posterior dislocation
Excessive anteversion Anterior dislocation
Excessive abduction (vertical, high theta) Posterosuperior dislocation · eccentric PE wear, late instability
Excessive adduction (horizontal) Flexion impingement, inferior dislocation

Cup medialization↓ body-weight moment arm → ↓ JRF ✓ (needs ↑ femoral offset to keep abductor tension) · not possible with resurfacing

AIIS hypertrophyimpingement + instability in straight flexion → resect · ✓ direct head of rectus femoris arises from AIIS (reflected head — groove above acetabular brim; sartorius — ASIS)

Spinopelvic mobility & cup position

Normal standing → sittingpelvis tilts posteriorly 20–35° (15–20°) · femur flexes 55–70° · sacral slope change 10–30° (11–29°) · pelvic-femoral angle change 51–69° · sitting anteinclination 41–63° · standing PFA 165–195° · sitting CSI 162–198°

Stiff spine✓ Δ sacral slope <10° → hip hypermobility → ↑ dislocation · every 1° ↓ spinopelvic motion → 0.9° ↑ femoral motion

Phenotype Pelvis Impingement → dislocation
Stuck sitting (APP tilted back 10–13°) Fixed posterior tilt Posterior impingement → ANTERIOR dislocation ✓ (even via posterior approach, if combined anteversion excessive)
Stuck standing (APP neutral) Fails to tilt back when sitting Anterior impingement → POSTERIOR dislocation

Stiff-spine targetsLum: inclination 45–50°, anteversion 20–25°, combined 35–40° · McKnight (stuck sitting): less inclination (35–40°) + less anteversion (15–20°) · large head / dual mobility, restore offset (high-offset stem), navigation/robotics

5Management

Femoral offset & abductor tension

Femoral offset✓ perpendicular distance from head centre to femoral shaft axis (line 4) · horizontal offset (label B) most affects JRF (neck length also ↑ offset but lengthens leg; vertical height = length only)

↑ Offset ↓ Offset
↓ impingement · ↓ JRF · ↑ soft-tissue tension without ↑ length · ↑ stability · ↓ wear, ↓ cup strain, ↓ limp Instability · abductor weakness · gluteus medius lurch / Trendelenburg · ✓ ↑ osseous (bony) impingement · ↑ JRF
Risk: lateral prominence → trochanteric bursitis ↓ bursitis risk

High-offset stem✓ ↑ soft-tissue tension (✗ Wrong options: ↑ JRF · ↑ length · ↑ cup loosening (that is lateralized liner) · ↑ dislocation) · ✓ improves stability by ↑ abductor tension (✗ Wrong options: shorter neck · low offset · larger head · medialized cup)

Exacerbates Trendelenburg✓ decreasing femoral offset
✗ Wrong options: extended offset neck · bigger head · longer neck · inferior cup

↓ JRF✓ medialize cup or ↑ offset
✗ Wrong options: ↑ NSA · ↓ offset · ↑ femoral anteversion · head-neck ratio (stability only)

Ways to ↑ offsetlonger neck · ↓ NSA · medialize neck + lengthen · trochanteric advancement · lateralized liner

Soft-tissue function

System Conditions impairing stability
Central nervous Stroke, cerebellar disease, dementia, MS, Parkinson, myelopathy, delirium, alcoholism

THA Trunnionosis

Recon · 36 / 65

1Basics

Definitionmechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC) · metal ion release from corrosion at the femoral head–neck Morse taper → hip pain + adverse local tissue reaction (ALTR)

Occurs with any bearing✓ metal-on-polyethylene as well as MoM · relatively rare · lucency between head and cup = PE liner → not MoM
✗ Wrong options: only in MoM

Modularitylets surgeon tune length + offset · extra junction = corrosion site · dual-modular (modular neck) stems → two junctions (head–neck + neck–stem) → fretting corrosion most common failure → revise to monoblock stem

Risk factors

Factor ↑ Corrosion ↓ Corrosion
Head size ✓ Larger CoCr heads (↑ torque on trunnion) Smaller heads
Trunnion geometry ✓ Shorter, thinner taper (flexible, ↓ interference fit, ↑ micromotion, edge loading) Longer, wider, more rigid taper
Materials ✓ Mixed alloy taper/bore (CoCr head on Ti stem) Similar alloy couple · ceramic head
Head length ✓ Long (high-length) heads Low-length heads
Stem High-offset stems (↑ fretting) · low-rigidity stems —
Assembly Impaction <4,000 N · wet taper · impaction off-axis 4,000 N, dry, in line with taper
Patient High BMI, ↑ cyclical loading —
Bearing MoM (ions contribute to taper wear) —

Cemented vs cementless fixationunrelated to trunnionosis

2Mechanism

Mechanism – fretting & crevice corrosion

Type Mechanism
Galvanic Electrochemical electron transfer between dissimilar metals in conductive medium (CoCr head on Ti stem)
Fretting ✓ Micromotion between two materials → wear + ion release · disrupts passivation (oxide) layer · ✓ micromotion at head–neck junction → fretting · commonest in modular necks
Crevice / pitting Physicochemical metal–environment interaction · low-O₂ area anodic, O₂-rich cathodic · in fatigue cracks · 316L stainless steel most prone, titanium least
MACC Fretting + crevice combined → passivation layer breaks, O₂-rich fluid enters crevices, acidic layer, ↑ ions → catastrophic failure

Self-passivationTi and CoCr form adherent oxide coat → protective
✗ Wrong options: cause of symptoms

Adhesive wearPE adheres to bearing → osteolysis
✗ Wrong options: a corrosion type in trunnionosis

Tissue responseALVAL / pseudotumour = lymphocyte-mediated (type IV) · same as MoM · macrophages → PE debris osteolysis · neutrophils → infection

3Presentation

Symptomspain + limp commonest · delayed groin/buttock/thigh pain · "clunking"

Exampalpable pseudocyst if ALTR large · abductor weakness / Trendelenburg (attritional abductor destruction by ARMD) — not primary avulsion

Catastrophic failuresudden pop, inability to walk → head–neck dissociation / stem fracture at trunnion · not dislocation from failed precautions

4Diagnosis & Classification

Key radiology findings

RadiographsAP + lateral · ✓ may be normal · osteolysis (calcar, GT) late · Judet / CT if advanced osteolysis

MARS MRIperiarticular pseudotumour, fluid collection, capsular thickening, soft-tissue destruction · US — fluid collection adjacent to joint

Genes & lab markers

Rule out infection firstESR, CRP, WBC · aspiration with ✓ manual cell count (metal debris falsely ↑ automated count)
✗ Wrong options: automated count confirms

Metal ions✓ cobalt ↑ much more than chromium · no pathognomonic level

Co : Cr ratio
Trunnionosis ≥2:1 (Orthobullets) · ~5:1 / Co 4–5× Cr (OB explanations)
MoM bearing wear ~1:1 (1–2:1)

Cobalt threshold for MACC work-up>1 ng/mL (ppb) (Orthobullets; OB: MoP with ions >1.0 µg/L) · ≥1.6 ng/mL suggested (OB) — read the options

Elevated serum cobalt✓ expected with CoCr head + fluid collection
✗ Wrong options: pedestal (loosening) · macrophages (PE) · HO · LLD

5Management

Suspected trunnionosis
  • Asymptomatic→observe
  • Infection not excluded→manual cell count, aspiration
  • Painful, infection excluded→single-stage revision
    • Stem + cup well fixed→ceramic head + Ti sleeve + new PE liner
    • Taper grossly damaged / stem failed→revise stem + ceramic head + new liner

Revision – ceramic head with titanium sleeve

Indicationpainful THA + risk factors + Co elevated > Cr, no infection

Techniquefrozen sections + cultures · extensive synovectomy / debridement (remove metal debris, devitalised tissue → prevents recurrence) · inspect + clean taper · retain vs revise stem

Head✓ ceramic head with titanium sleeve · sleeve prevents ceramic fracture on damaged taper
✗ Wrong options: CoCr → CoCr (recurrent ALTR) · CoCr + sleeve

Liner✓ always exchange (embedded metal debris)

Lowest recurrence✓ ceramic-on-polyethylene

Prevention✓ ceramic femoral head eliminates CoCr–Ti interaction
✗ Wrong options: larger head · cemented fixation · diaphyseal stem

Scenario Answer
Large CoCr head, black fluid, Co 12/Cr 2, manual WBC 1,500 ✓ ceramic head + Ti sleeve + new PE (✗ Wrong options: revise both components · spacer · bursa injection)
Intra-op corroded trunnion, well-fixed parts ✓ ceramic head + Ti sleeve (✗ Wrong options: I&D only (recurrence) · 2-stage · IV antibiotics · cup revision)
Mild trunnion damage, 44 mm CoCr head ✓ clean trunnion + ceramic head + Ti sleeve + liner exchange (✗ Wrong options: remove all components)
Catastrophic stem/trunnion failure, cup fixed ✓ revise femoral component + ceramic head + new liner (✗ Wrong options: observe · ions first · sleeve only · revise cup)
Modular-neck stem with ALTR Revise entire femoral component to monoblock

Cells Lymphocytes Lymphocytes Macrophages Neutrophils

Type Cause Treatment

Definitionflexion gap > extension gap · PS knee can "jump the post" → dislocation

✗ Wrong options: tight flexion gap

Loose flexion gap, normal extension gap (PS) → ✓ posterior knee dislocation (cam locked behind/in front of post)
✗ Wrong options: MUA · hyperextension (loose extension gap) · anterior dislocation · patella fracture (<13 mm patella)

Recurrent dislocation of PS mobile-bearing revision → ✓ loose flexion gap (undersized / anteriorised femur, excess distal augmentation, collateral + posterior capsule insufficiency)
✗ Wrong options: loose extension gap (V/V instability) · malrotation (patellar/rotational) · design

TKA Kinematic Alignment

Recon · 46 / 65

1Basics

DefinitionTKA that restores the patient's pre-arthritic limb alignment + joint lines by resurfacing distal femur and proximal tibia · ✓ "ligament-sparing" — bone cuts, not releases, recreate native laxity

Origin (TO)Howell and Hull (2008), "custom-fit positioning" · driven by ~20% dissatisfaction after mechanical alignment (TO)

Individualised approaches (TO)✓ kinematic + functional · fixed approaches = mechanical + anatomical
✗ Wrong options: anatomical as individualised

Anatomic rationale

HKA axis (varus / neutral / valgus) and joint-line obliquity (varus / neutral / valgus) are independent → 9 combinations

Only ~15% of knees have 180° HKA with joint line perpendicular → MA alters ~85% of patients

Native alignment (TO / OB)

Measure Value
Distal femur 0–4° valgus (to mechanical axis) · ~9° valgus to vertical
Femoral anatomic vs mechanical axis 4–6° valgus (OB) · 6° (TO)
Proximal tibia 1–5° varus · ~3° varus to midline
Overall limb Slight varus ~3°
Joint line ~3° varus (flexion + extension)
Tibial slope 1–9° posterior

Foundational principles

Arthritisminimal femoral bone wear · minimal ligament contracture/attenuation · PCL usually intact · varus/valgus deformity = cartilage loss + tibial wear

Balancelaxity least in extension · in flexion lateral more lax than medial · avoid joint-line elevation/depression (baja/alta)

The three kinematic axes of the femur

Axis Description
Flexion–extension (cylindrical) Transverse axis across distal femur about which tibia flexes · oriented differently from TEA (Orthobullets) · same as TEA (TO) — read the options
Internal–external rotation Longitudinal axis in medial compartment (medial pivot) · tibial IR in flexion → lateral condyle roll-back
Patellar tracking Isometric axis across medial condyle · analogous to Schöttle point (MPFL)

All threeparallel or perpendicular to the native femoral joint line → resurfacing femur restores them

✗ Wrong options: mechanical HKA (changed by arthritis) · LDFA · MPTA alone

JLO 180 ± 3° <177° (apex distal) >183° (apex proximal)

Surgical technique

Femoral target✓ femoral component condyle thickness − 1 mm (saw kerf) − 2 mm (cartilage loss)

Tibial balancingafter femoral resurfacing, adjust tibial varus/valgus + slope · no soft-tissue releases · no PCL sacrifice/recession · TO: only tibial cut used to balance (plus osteophytes, posterior capsule off femur, tibial ML shift)

Method Pros Cons
Caliper-verified Any instruments/implant · cuts within ±0.5 mm of target Sagittal femoral flexion hard with IM rod · tibial recuts common · sizing hard pre-op

KA versus MA

Varus kneesvarus tibial cuts / residual varus ✓ not associated with bony or hardware failure

Valgus knees (KA view)no hypoplastic LFC · natural valgus joint line with comparable condyles · lateral cartilage + tibial wear (contrast: conventional teaching = LFC hypoplasia)

RotationER of femur/tibia not needed for tracking · many native trochleae are IR relative to TEA · tracking from correct HKA, JLO, joint-line height + tubercle IR in flexion

Implantmedial-pivot design needed for normal kinematics · concern about shear on PS cam-post

Outcomes (OB)loosening, reoperation equal · satisfaction + ROM equal or better

Controversies (TO)needs PSI/technology · ACL + menisci sacrificed · non-weight-bearing kinematics differ · no limits on outliers → restrict to mild deformity · few long-term data

Related techniques

Technique Principle
Restricted KA Limits on component + HKA varus/valgus · safe zone (TO): LDFA + MPTA 86–93°, final mHKA −5° varus to +4° valgus · minor releases rather than exceed limits
Functional alignment Adjust femoral + tibial cuts in all 3 planes for symmetric/asymmetric gaps · no releases · e.g. tibia up to 3° varus for tight medial extension · femoral IR for tight lateral flexion · limb within 0 ± 3°
Inverse KA Predetermined tibial cut → femur gap-balanced · no releases
Anatomical (Hungerford 1982) Tibia 3° varus + femur extra 3° valgus (7–10° total) · for CR · risks asymmetric poly wear, LCL/popliteus damage (TO)
Mechanical (Freeman & Swanson 1973) Both components ⊥ mechanical axis · releases balance gaps · varus knee: more lateral tibia + more distal/posterior MFC removed → MCL tight · 15–20% remain symptomatic (TO)

Supplyanastomotic ring · ✓ medial-sided vessels contribute more than lateral

Step Vascularity disrupted
Medial arthrotomy 0–35%
Fat pad excision 0–16% (anterior tibial recurrent a. + inferior ring, not medial/lateral vessels)
Lateral release 53–75% (superior + inferior lateral geniculates)
✓ Medial arthrotomy + lateral release 50–100% (OB option) · up to 75% (Orthobullets/OB text)
Lateral meniscectomy Does not disrupt ring

View Finding

History

Era Milestone
19th c Soft-tissue interposition

1958 MacIntosh & McKeever — acrylic tibial plateau

Femoral rollback✓ posterior translation of the femur with flexion → ↑ quad lever arm + flexion by preventing posterior impingement in deep flexion (TO) · native: controlled by ACL + PCL · CR: native PCL · PS: tibial post contacts femoral cam

ConstraintV/V + F/E stability despite ligament laxity or bone loss · more constraint → more force to fixation → aseptic loosening

Least → most constrained

Modularitymetal tray + modular insert, augments, stems · customise intra-op · but ↑ osteolysis + backside wear (micromotion insert–tray) · more expensive

Kinematics (medial pivot, paradoxical motion)

Native knee✓ femur pivots about a medial axis in flexion (lateral condyle rolls back more: larger radius / convex lateral plateau) · flexion → femoral ER (tibial IR) + rollback · terminal extension → femur IR, lateral condyle translates anteriorly (screw-home = tibial ER last 15°) · lateral condyle posterior 12.7 mm vs medial 2.9 mm (TO)

Paradoxical translation✓ anterior translation of tibiofemoral contact point from extension → flexion · commonest in CR (no ACL, posterior resting point; PCL not tight until ~45°) · also PS before cam engages · CR shows it in first **~40°**

Medial-pivot / medial-stabilised / medial congruent (MC)✓ ball-and-socket medial (spherical single-radius MFC), less congruent lateral → lateral rollback · asymmetric liner · raised anterior lip · higher PROMs in some studies

NOT true of medial pivot (TO)✓ "spherical variable radius MFC" (it is single radius)

Flexion → extension in medial-congruent design → ✓ medial pivot, femur internally rotates + translates anteriorly

Insert truths✓ standard CR can show paradoxical anterior femoral translation · AS lip prevents femur rolling forward when PCL weak (✗ Wrong options: replaces ACL) · dual-pivot = lateral pivot early, medial pivot deep · mobile bearing (✗ Wrong options: medial pivot) has insert–tray motion · PS promotes rollback (✗ Wrong options: minimises)

1Basics

Overview

Osteolysishistiocytic (macrophage) response to wear debris → bone loss · same biology as aseptic loosening, faster + focal

4 steps(1) particulate debris formation → (2) macrophage-activated osteoclastogenesis + osteolysis → (3) prosthesis micromotion → (4) particulate debris dissemination

Aseptic loosening✓ commonest cause of late THA failure · supra-acetabular osteolysis usually >10 yr after index surgery · ↓ since HXLPE

Closest correlate of osteolysis → ✓ linear wear rate of the bearing couple · activity, cup position, PE oxidation, bearing all act by ↑ wear
✗ Wrong options: weight · head material · offset

Wear mechanisms (adhesion, abrasion, backside wear)

Mechanism What happens Key fact
Adhesive Surfaces bond under load → weaker material (PE) pulled off ✓ Most common / most important in THA osteolysis (TO)
Abrasive (two-body) Harder, rough surface cuts softer — cheese grater Rough head scratches PE · ploughing, cutting, fragmentation
Third-body Trapped particles between bearing surfaces Type of abrasive wear · PMMA mainly (bone, metal beads, HA, Al oxide, BaSO₄, taper corrosion debris)
Fatigue / delamination Cyclic subsurface stress → microcracks, pits → large particles ✓ TKA PE failure (TO) — max stress just below surface
Fretting Small oscillation between surfaces not meant to move Backside wear (shell–liner, tray–insert)
Corrosive Sliding in corrosive / oxidative environment —

Hip vs knee PEhip: ✓ adhesion + abrasion at the surface · knee: fatigue cracking + delamination
✗ Wrong options: fretting · crevice corrosion (under screw heads) · oxidative for hip

Third-body wear — NOT true → ✓ "particle size more important than hardness" (TO) · hardness / composition, concentration matter more · implant hardness <0.8× particle → severe abrasion · >1.2× → resistant · vitamin E PE has better surface properties

Wear modes (McKellop)1: bearing surfaces as intended · 2: bearing vs non-bearing surface · 3: third body between bearing surfaces · 4: two non-bearing surfaces

Wear stagesprimary (run-in) → secondary (steady state; most of life) → tertiary (rapid failure)

Determinants of wear → wear factor, sliding distance, load — ✓ all independent determinants (TO)

PE cup wear pattern sequence → ✓ foldings first (loading force) → ripples (loading-shear; adhesive; slowly worn cups) → fibrils (abrasive; rapidly worn cups) (TO)
✗ Wrong options: fibrils · ripples · ditches

Optimally positioned cup — wear site → ✓ anterosuperior quadrant (TO) · excess inclination ↑ edge wear · greatly anteverted cup → posterior (neck impingement in extension)

Linear vs volumetric wear

Linear wear Volumetric wear
Definition Head penetration into the liner (thickness lost) Total volume removed → ✓ number of particles
Measure Livermore — shortest distance head centre → acetabular surface V = πr²w (∝ radius² of head)
Main factor Orthobullets: independent of head size · TO: 22 mm > 32 mm — read the options ✓ Head size · total contact area (TO)
Failure Wear-through of PE cup Osteolysis
Threshold >0.1 mm/yr → osteolysis + loosening (rare below) —

Head size22 mm: ↑ linear, ↓ volumetric, ↑ central wear + dislocation · 32 mm: ↓ linear, ↑ volumetric, thinner PE, ↑ ROM · 28 mm = compromise → most systems (TO)

Conventional PE32 mm heads significantly more volumetric wear than 22 or 26/28 mm · 1 mm ↑ head size → ~10% ↑ volumetric wear

HXLPEwear independent of head size 22–46 mm → 32 vs 28 mm = ✓ equivalent wear · head >40 mm no proven longevity gain
✗ Wrong options: ↑ dislocation · ↓ ROM · ↓ osteolysis · ↑ periprosthetic fracture

Bearing Wear rate / particles

Particle type & size

Commonest particle✓ UHMWPE (up to 90% of debris volume; colourless, mostly spheroid) · also PMMA, Al oxide, Zr oxide, CoCr, Ti, third body

Size implicated✓ <1 µm (submicron), 0.1–1 µm · mean PE 0.5 µm, metal 0.7 µm (Maloney) · most stimulatory 0.2–7/8 µm · most particles <5 µm, random shape (TO) · active 0.5–10 µm (TO)
✗ Wrong options: 10, 100, 1000 µm
